new_statements.quote: De toon komt meestal op de laatste syllabe, in drielettergrepige woorden op de eerste, met een bijtoon op de laatste; als we menen de toon te moeten aangeven, doen we dat door middel van een accent grave.
new_statements.translation: The stress mostly falls on the last syllable, in trisyllabic words on the first, with a secondary stress on the last; when we think the stress needs to be indicated, we do so by means of a grave accent.
new_statements.citation: Drabbe, Peter. 1950. Talen en Dialecten van Zuid-West Nieuw-Guinea [Deel I]. Anthropos 45: 545-574.
new_statements.locator: Part II 'Mombum', sec. 36 'Klinkers en Medeklinkers', p. 562 (verified on page scan)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (the scanned text) and the rendered page scan Anthropos 45, p. 562, sec. 36 'Klinkers en Medeklinkers'). The sentence is there exactly as quoted: 'De toon komt meestal op de laatste syllabe, in drielettergrepige woorden op de eerste, met een bijtoon op de laatste; als we menen de toon te moeten aangeven, doen we dat door middel van een accent grave.' (scanned has 'jaatste' for 'laatste'; the image reads 'laatste'). Translation in the report is accurate ('toon' = stress/accent here, as Drabbe uses it throughout his sketches). Identity: sec. 35 (p. 561, scanned read) says the Mombum-taal (Mombum-taghanan) is spoken only in one small village of 220 souls on Komolom island, village/tribe…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is usually final; trisyllabic words are said to take main stress on the first syllable with a secondary stress on the final syllable. Stress is impressionistic ('toon'), marked ad hoc with a grave accent in the sketch and the 422-item wordlist; the graves there are mostly final (Mombùm, taghanàn, iröwè, maràw, ghorughùr) but also initial (ìdumu, dàghana-, tèghe, ndàu) and medial (kerèndjeram, kemunùmuri), so placement is not fully predictable from the stated rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: In trisyllabic words with initial main stress, a secondary stress ('bijtoon') on the last syllable. (Geurtjens 1933: [397], blanket note for his bordering-language lists incl. Komelomsch: secondary stress alternates trochaically leftward from the final main stress.)
new_statements.exceptions: 'meestal' (mostly) final; trisyllables initial. No lexical exceptions listed, but grave-marked forms in the wordlist deviate in both directions (trisyllabic ghorughùr, pegherù with final grave; disyllabic tèghe, ndàu with initial grave).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, citation forms from a brief missionary sketch (single village, 220 speakers, 1950); no phrase-level discussion; author hedges by marking stress only 'when we think it necessary'. Supporting blanket statement in Geurtjens 1933: [397] ('De hoofdklemtoon valt steeds op de laatste lettergreep..') covers Komelomsch (= Mombum) among other lists but is not Mombum-specific. Voorhoeve 1975: 397 wrongly reports 'no rules of stress placement have been given'.
new_statements.identity_note: Drabbe 1950 describes 'Mombùm(-taghanàn)', the language of the single village Mombum/Komolom on Komolom Island (220 speakers in 1950) = Glottolog nucl1452 Mombum [mso] exactly (not the sister language Koneraw kone1234). Geurtjens 1933's 'Komelomsch' list is the same variety, but his stress note is a blanket remark covering all his bordering-language lists.

sources.note: Blanket note for all bordering-language wordlists (Komelomsch included), p. [397]: 'De hoofdklemtoon valt steeds op de laatste lettergreep, tenzij deze een toonlooze uitgang is.. (breve); Van de laatste lettergreep verspringt de bijklemtoon trocheevormig naar voren. In 't Digoeleesch valt de klemtoon vaak op de voorlaatste.' Final main stress, trochaic secondary leftward; not Mombum-specific.
